frameworks.name: Three P's Framework
frameworks.definition: Three origin buckets for business ideas: Pain (personal problem overcome), Profession (day-job skill), and Passion (deep personal interest).

frameworks.name: Mosey Money Mad Lib
frameworks.definition: A sentence-completion template for articulating a business offer: 'I help [who] get [good stuff] without [bad stuff] through [unique mechanism].'

frameworks.name: Unique Mechanism
frameworks.definition: A proprietary named process or system (checklist or sequential steps) that differentiates a solution from competitors and anchors a prospect's hope of success.

frameworks.name: Warm Outreach First-Five-Customers System
frameworks.definition: A structured cold-to-warm contact script: greet, give specific compliment, state one-sentence offer, ask if they know anyone who needs it; repeat for four hours per day or 100 contacts per day.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that picking any business idea immediately is better than waiting to pick the perfect one, because zero-feedback ideation cannot produce a correct first pick; the iteration loop that follows the first pick is the mechanism by which any bad idea becomes a good one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has zero customer feedback
first-business context
claims.mechanism: Picking any idea initiates real-market feedback; repeated refinements make the idea progressively less wrong until it is viable. Without a first pick, no feedback loop starts.
bounded_by: Does not claim the first pick will succeed on its own without iteration

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that narrower avatar specificity enables proportionally higher pricing: a broad time-management product commands ~$19, a time-management product for salespeople commands ~$199, one for outbound salespeople commands ~$1,999, and one for outbound garden-and-power-tools salespeople can command ~$10,000, because hyper-specificity signals expert knowledge of the customer's exact context and eliminates all competition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: information or coaching products
each narrower tier assumes the same underlying content
claims.mechanism: Ultra-specific positioning eliminates competitors and signals deep insider knowledge of the customer's context, removing price anchors set by generalist alternatives.

anchors.region: industry-role-specific (outbound garden and power tools salespeople)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that starting a business to serve people like yourself (a personal pain you overcame) produces more committed, higher-quality operators than starting from pure market analysis, because founders who share the customer's pain know the intricacies of that pain without research and will care more about delivering exceptional results over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: first business
founder has personally experienced the target problem
claims.mechanism: Shared pain provides automatic customer empathy and precise pain description without interviews; that empathy sustains commitment through the difficult early phase when market-analysts (mercenaries) quit.
bounded_by: Does not claim market-analysis-driven businesses cannot succeed, only that they produce mercenary rather than missionary founders

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a very specific pain point description bypasses advertising blindness and banner ad skepticism more effectively than a broad benefit claim, because specificity signals the speaker shares the prospect's lived experience rather than selling a generic solution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: cold-audience advertising or copywriting
founder serving an avatar they personally belong to
claims.mechanism: Specific pain language (e.g., 'stop feeling your thighs chafing in the sun') passes the prospect's mental filter because it matches a real recalled sensation, whereas broad claims ('lose weight fast') trigger learned skepticism from decades of over-promised marketing.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the two and only two levers available to motivate a prospect to act are: (1) moving them toward desired good outcomes, and (2) moving them away from unwanted bad outcomes; all effective copywriting and sales is a combination of these two levers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ultra-hyper-specific niche positioning effectively eliminates competition because competitors rarely inhabit positions that specific, allowing the first mover at that specificity level to set their own price without facing market alternatives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: information, coaching, or professional services
niche defined by 4+ intersecting attributes
claims.mechanism: When a product is uniquely positioned at the intersection of a specific role, problem, and industry, no direct comparable exists for the buyer to price-compare against, giving the seller a monopoly on that specific need.
bounded_by: Assumes the niche has sufficient addressable buyers to sustain a business

examples.text: A friend's wife with nine children realized that her daily system for making lunches for all nine kids was a business-worthy process: she organized individual labeled bags, optimized for cost, and ensured nutritional requirements were met within a constrained time window. Hormozi used this to illustrate how a personal operational pain — one so embedded in daily life it is invisible — can become the seed of a business when named and systematized.

A registered dietitian who worked six days a week and twelve-plus hours per day at a hospital had only one day per week available to bill private clients, forcing her to master complex insurance billing in compressed time. She turned that narrow hard-won skill into a teaching business for other registered dietitians. With only 5,800 Instagram followers, she earns nearly $1 million per year in income — demonstrating that a hyper-specific professional skill taught to the same profession can generate seven-figure income from a tiny audience.

Alex Hormozi described his first dollar earned: a woman at his gym asked for help with her diet because he looked in shape. They met at a pizza shop where he asked what she was buying for groceries and gave her protein-focused recipes. After about ninety minutes, she pulled out her checkbook unprompted and wrote him a $100 check without being pitched, without a stated price, and without a formal sales process. Walking out to the parking lot, he opened the check and realized for the first time that someone would pay him for fitness knowledge. He identifies this woman — Sandy Smith — as the origin of his business journey.

Sarah Blakely identified a personal frustration — that available undergarments did not hide unflattering contours while showing flattering ones — and built Spanx around that single personal pain. Spanx ultimately sold to Blackstone for approximately $1 billion, illustrating that solving a personal problem that maps to a large population's unstated frustration can produce an enterprise-scale business.

P90X used the term 'muscle confusion' as its unique mechanism — a proprietary framing of varied workout sequences — despite fitness experts widely agreeing that muscle confusion as a physiological concept does not exist. Nevertheless, P90X sold hundreds of millions of dollars in fitness programs. Weight Watchers uses its 'point system' as its unique mechanism. Hormozi cites these examples to argue that the named proprietary process — not the underlying scientific validity — is what converts prospects by giving them a vehicle to attach their hope of success.

Hormozi illustrated avatar narrowing with a time-management product: sold broadly to anyone, it commands roughly $19. Sold specifically to salespeople, it commands ~$199. Targeted at outbound salespeople, ~$1,999. Targeted at outbound salespeople in the garden and power tools industry, ~$10,000 — because a buyer in that niche knows they can recoup the cost from a single additional deal, and no competitors exist at that specificity level.

practices.text: Use the Mosey Money Mad Lib template to construct your initial offer sentence: 'I help [three-attribute avatar] get [desired outcome] without [feared bad outcome].' Add a named unique mechanism once you have completed at least one iteration of the process.

Conduct customer-discovery interviews before writing copy by asking: What problems are you struggling with right now? How long have you had them? What makes it painful specifically? What would your ideal experience look like? What have you had to stop doing that you like? What have you had to start doing that you hate?

Name your proprietary process using alliteration or rhyme to make it memorable and sticky; the named process becomes your unique mechanism and the primary differentiator against competitors who serve the same avatar.

For warm outreach to get the first five customers: greet the contact, give a genuine specific compliment, state your one-sentence offer, and ask whether they know anyone who could benefit. Repeat for four hours per day or 100 contacts per day, whichever comes first.
